one_line: A feature tour of Windsurf's Cascade and Flows agent features, comparing it with Cursor and building a 2048 game and a Splitwise clone from single prompts. Useful as a demo of full-stack generation, thin on technical depth.
summary: The video is an 8-minute walkthrough of Windsurf (Codeium's AI editor), focused on its Flows feature, which merges agent and copilot behaviour: it plans, works through steps, and keeps context when told to continue. The host tests Cascade, Windsurf's counterpart to Cursor Composer, by generating a playable 2048 game, changing its colours with a follow-up prompt, and reviewing the edits through the OpenDiff button. He then asks for a Splitwise clone, which the agent scaffolds with Bootstrap 5 templates, a database, and auto-fixes, though a routing error needed the pasted error message to resolve. The host reports that the generated app lacked back/forward navigation and that Cursor shows edits live while writing, which he prefers. Pricing is presented as cheaper than Cursor with a more generous free tier, but these are the host's claims without sources. Overall the video is a demo-driven tour with little architecture or evaluation content.

key_ideas.idea: Flows merges agents and copilots: a prompt produces a plan, then the agent works through steps while you review progress.
key_ideas.detail: Saying 'continue' resumes with the earlier context retained, which the host says behaves like an agent. The feature is presented as the standout versus Cursor.

key_ideas.idea: Cascade is the Composer equivalent and can start from built-in example projects.
key_ideas.detail: The host picks the first example (a playable 2048 app with smooth animations). Cascade creates a folder, writes the code, and gives run instructions. A follow-up colour-change prompt was applied correctly.

key_ideas.idea: Edits are reviewed after the fact via OpenDiff, not streamed live.
key_ideas.detail: OpenDiff opens each changed file with its edits. The host says Cursor Composer is better here because it shows changes as they are written.

key_ideas.idea: A single name-based prompt ('build Splitwise') produced a full-stack scaffold: HTML templates in Bootstrap 5, then a database when asked to implement all features.
key_ideas.detail: The host notes that other editors often fail to clone or build a popular app from its name. He suspects Windsurf may have pre-built instructions for Splitwise, which he does not verify.

key_ideas.idea: Runtime errors were fixed by pasting the raw error into Cascade, which diagnosed a routing problem.
key_ideas.detail: The agent first tried to fix a 'not found' error itself and failed twice. The pasted error led to the correct diagnosis and a working app.

key_ideas.idea: Generated apps can miss basics: the Splitwise clone had no back/forward navigation, so the host used the browser's buttons.
key_ideas.detail: Group creation, adding members by email, and expense tracking did work in the demo. The host calls navigation a gap to improve.

key_ideas.idea: Pricing and free-tier claims favour Windsurf, but are stated without sources in the video.
key_ideas.detail: The host says Windsurf's Pro plan is about half the price of Cursor's roughly $20 plan, that Cursor's trial gives 200 completions and 50 slow premium requests, and that Windsurf's free tier includes unlimited autocomplete and editor chat.

techniques.name: Start from an example project in Cascade
techniques.how: Open the Cascade panel (Ctrl+L), choose one of the example projects offered, and let it create the folder and generate the app. The host picked a 2048 game with smooth animations, then ran the instructions Cascade printed.
techniques.when: Quick way to see the agent scaffold a small, self-contained app before using it on real work.

techniques.name: Iterative follow-up prompt, then review with OpenDiff
techniques.how: Give a targeted change in Cascade (for example, 'change the colours to green and yellow'). When it finishes, press OpenDiff to inspect every file changed and the exact edits before accepting.
techniques.when: Making a small, reviewable change to generated code where you want a per-file diff rather than live streaming.

techniques.name: Name-based full-stack build prompt
techniques.how: Ask for a known app by name ('build Splitwise'), then answer its follow-up questions (for example, 'proceed with the HTML templates', then 'implement all of them'). The agent adds templates, then the database.
techniques.when: Prototyping a multi-page app from one prompt. Expect to debug the output.

techniques.name: Paste raw errors back into the agent
techniques.how: When the app fails to start, copy the exact error text into Cascade rather than describing it. The agent inspects the app config and identifies the cause, here a routing bug.
techniques.when: Debugging generated code where the agent's own troubleshooting has already failed.

techniques.name: Flows for multi-step tasks with context kept
techniques.how: Give a multi-step prompt in Flows so it plans first. If it stops, reply 'continue' so it resumes from the retained context rather than starting over.
techniques.when: Longer builds where you want to watch the plan and resume mid-task without re-explaining.

tools: Claude models (named as available on Windsurf Pro, no version given)

numbers.claim: Windsurf Pro is said to cost half of Cursor's Pro plan, which the host puts at around $20 a month.
Cursor's free trial is described as 200 completions and 50 slow premium requests; its Pro plan as 500 fast premium requests.
Windsurf's free tier is described as having unlimited autocomplete and editor chat, even without Cascade. Windsurf Pro is described as giving unlimited access to Claude and GPT-4 models.
Windsurf Pro comes with a two-week trial, as Cursor does.
Video runtime is 8:39. The 2048 and Splitwise builds were sped up on screen, so generation times are not shown.

hot_takes: The host says Cursor Composer beats Windsurf because it shows changes live as it writes, while Windsurf only offers OpenDiff after the fact.
The host suspects Windsurf has pre-built instructions for Splitwise, which would make the 'build a popular app by name' demo less impressive. He does not verify this.
The host calls the one-prompt database generation something he has never seen before. This is his subjective impression and is not benchmarked.
The 'Better Than Cursor?' title is answered only by a feature tour with no timing, error-rate or cost measurements, so the verdict rests on one anecdotal run.

relevance.why: Consumer-facing IDE feature tour. Nothing about the self-hosted proxy, budgets, retrieval, serving or storage.
Flows' plan-then-step loop with a 'continue' to resume retained context loosely parallels ProsHarness checkpoint/resume and plan-driven runs. It is a product comparison, not a technique we can reuse.
relevance.action: Optional: when designing ProsHarness checkpoint/resume, compare how a plan-first run stores its state against what 'continue' keeps in context. This is reading, not a code change.
